Militaristic describes a strong, often excessive belief that military power is the most important tool a nation, person, or group can have — and that it should be used aggressively, proudly, and often, even in situations where peaceful solutions exist.

When something is described as militaristic, it means military force sits at the very center of how a person, government, or culture thinks and acts. The military is not treated as a cautious last resort, but as something to be glorified, expanded, and reached for first — even as the default answer to nearly every problem.

A country is militaristic when it pours enormous resources into its military — even at the cost of education, healthcare, or diplomacy — and when it consistently turns to force or intimidation to handle disputes rather than seeking peaceful negotiation. A culture is militaristic when it treats soldiers and conquest as the highest ideals of society, glorifying war as noble and honorable above all else. A policy is militaristic when it favors invasion, threat, or coercion over conversation and cooperation. A leader is militaristic when they speak in terms of domination, crushing enemies, and expanding power through force.

The key idea running through all of these is excess and aggression — a worldview where strength means military strength, and where military strength is the answer to everything.

This is one of the most important distinctions to understand about the word.

"Military" simply refers to anything related to armed forces — neutral descriptions of soldiers, warfare, or defense. A nation having a military is perfectly normal. A documentary about soldiers is a military documentary. There is no judgment in the word.

"Militaristic," on the other hand, is a judgment. It means going beyond what is reasonable or necessary — an obsessive, aggressive overvaluing of military power. Not just having strength, but making that strength an ideology, a source of pride, and the default solution to every challenge.

Here is a simple way to think about it: having a kitchen knife is completely normal. Insisting that the kitchen knife is the solution to every problem in your life — and spending all day sharpening it — is extreme. In the same way, having a military is normal. Being militaristic is treating the military as though it is the answer to everything.
The Tone and Connotation of the Word

Militaristic is almost always used in a critical or negative way. When someone calls a government, policy, or person militaristic, they are expressing concern, disapproval, or alarm. The word implies that something has tipped past reasonable necessity into dangerous territory — that force is being celebrated or used in ways that are excessive or unjust.

This is why you will rarely, if ever, hear someone proudly calling themselves militaristic. Even governments that invest heavily in military power prefer to describe themselves as "strong," "defense-focused," or "security-conscious." The word "militaristic" is almost always said about someone, not by them.
What Can Be Described as Militaristic?

The word is flexible and can attach to many different things. A government can be militaristic in how it approaches foreign policy — for example: "The regime adopted an increasingly militaristic stance toward its neighbors." A society or culture can be militaristic in its values — ancient Sparta is the classic example, a civilization where boys began military training at age seven and the warrior was the highest ideal. A person can hold a militaristic worldview, always reaching for forceful solutions to problems. A speech, a policy, an organization, or an attitude can all be described as militaristic when they share that same quality of placing aggression and force above all else.

Militaristic exists on a spectrum. Something can be mildly militaristic — slightly overemphasizing military solutions or spending a disproportionate amount on defense — or it can be extremely militaristic, with an entire society organized around the military. Imperial Japan before and during World War II is one of history's most extreme examples: the military effectively controlled the government, war was glorified as deeply honorable, and citizens were expected to sacrifice everything for conquest. Nazi Germany followed a similarly extreme militaristic ideology, treating military expansion as a national purpose and destiny.

To bring it all together: militaristic means believing — usually to an excessive and dangerous degree — that military power is supreme. That it should be glorified, heavily funded, aggressively used, and treated as the primary solution to the world's problems. It is not simply about having a military or respecting soldiers. It is about an ideology that places force at the center of everything. The word almost always carries criticism with it, signaling that someone or something has taken that belief too far.
